Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Rule 1 satisfied: 11 passing, 0 failing.

**Naming evaluation (first priority)**

- `runScenario`, `runStep`, `quotePremium`, `roundPremium`, `sumOfItemBasePremiums` — all clearly reveal intent. Keep.
- `formsRuneBlock` — accurate today (rune-specific), but the name says "rune" while the constants say `COMPONENT_BLOCK_*`. It is honest about the current behaviour, and per the instruction I must not generalise ahead of the test. Keep.
- `policyBasePremiumFor` — reads fine at the call site (`policyBasePremiumFor(items)`). Keep.
- `COMPONENT_BLOCK_SIZE` / `COMPONENT_BLOCK_PREMIUM` — fine.

One genuine intent problem: `sumOfItemBasePremiums` does `BASE_PREMIUMS[item.type]` on a `Record<string, number>`, which TypeScript types as `number` even for an unknown type where it is actually `undefined`. That is a lie in the types, silently producing `NaN`. The error-case test for unknown item types exists as a todo, so I will not add behaviour — but I can make the lookup honest without changing behaviour.

**APP mass, before** (`quotePremium` and its helpers):

- `sumOfItemBasePremiums`: bindings `items, sum, item` = 3; invocations `reduce`, `+`, index-lookup = 6; loop (reduce) = 5 → 14
- `formsRuneBlock`: constants `"rune"` = 1; bindings `items, item` = 2; invocations `filter`, `===`, `.type` compare, `===` size = 6; loop = 5 → 14
- `policyBasePremiumFor`: binding `items` = 1; invocations 2 = 4; conditional `?:` = 4 → 9
- `quotePremium`: bindings `items, policyBasePremium, firstInsuranceSurcharge` = 3; invocations `policyBasePremiumFor`, `roundPremium`, `*`, `+`, `+` = 10 → 13

Total ≈ 50.

The two named intermediate bindings in `quotePremium` are the cheap part (mass 1 each) and carry the domain vocabulary, so I keep them — Rule 2 trumps APP.

**Rule 4 (fewest elements)** — `policyBasePremiumFor` is a one-line indirection whose only job is the block conditional. Inlining it into `quotePremium` would remove an element, but it would put the block rule inside the surcharge arithmetic and blur two separate concerns. It also is the exact seam the next test (per-type grouping) will widen. Keep it.

So the refactoring I apply is the type-honesty one on the lookup:

content.text:
All 11 tests still pass and `tsc --noEmit` is clean.

**APP mass, after**: the extracted `basePremiumOf` adds a binding (1) plus one invocation at the call site (2), while removing the inline index-lookup invocation (2) from `sumOfItemBasePremiums`. Net ≈ 50 → 51, i.e. +1. This is a deliberate Rule 2 over APP trade: the cast is now confined to one named function that says what it does, instead of being an untyped index into a `Record<string, number>` in the middle of a reduce.

## Refactor summary

**Rule 1 (tests pass)**: green before and after, 11 passing / 38 todo.

**Rule 2 (reveals intent)** — the one change applied. `BASE_PREMIUMS` was typed `Record<string, number>`, which made `BASE_PREMIUMS[item.type]` type-check as `number` for *any* string, including unknown item types where the real value is `undefined` and the arithmetic silently yields `NaN`. The types were lying. It is now `as const satisfies Record<string, number>` with a derived `InsurableItemType` key union, and the lookup lives in a named `basePremiumOf(item)`. Behaviour is unchanged — the unknown-type case is still a todo test and I did not implement it — but the single remaining unsafe cast is now visible and named, so the future error-handling test has an obvious place to land.

**Rule 3 (no duplication)**: none found. `sumOfItemBasePremiums` and `formsRuneBlock` both traverse `items` but compute unrelated things; merging them would couple two rules that the next test is about to pull apart.

**Rule 4 (fewest elements)**: considered inlining `policyBasePremiumFor` (a one-line indirection, mass 9). Rejected — it isolates the block rule from the surcharge arithmetic, and it is exactly the seam the next test widens.

**Deliberately left alone**, per your instruction not to implement ahead of the test: `formsRuneBlock` is still rune-specific and still requires *exactly* 3 (so 4 and 7 runes correctly get no block). Its name is honest about that. When the "3 runes + 3 moonstones" test arrives it will want to become per-type grouping — group items by `type`, apply the block premium to each group of exactly 3, sum the rest — and the constants `COMPONENT_BLOCK_SIZE` / `COMPONENT_BLOCK_PREMIUM` are already named generically for that. I did not make that change.

Implementation file: `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-05_11-06-59_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.1.5-pure-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking-2/src/claim-office.ts`

One thing worth flagging for the next Red phase: the `Item.type` field is typed `string`, so the spec's unknown-item-type error tests are reachable, but `Customer.yearsWithMHPCO` is currently read by nothing at all — the loyalty-discount and follow-up-discount todos will be the first tests to exercise it, and `quotePremium` will need the customer threaded through to it.
